Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-12T00:33:00Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-12T00:33:02Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 6 minutes {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-12T00:26:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-12T00:34:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 58 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-12T00:36:01Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 0.9% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.1% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 1.5% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none beyond its normal variation - stretches as long before it began averaged as high on their own.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 215.51666666666668 ms {series_before} before it began, 1797.5 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 2210 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, average_spend_per_item loops over account.purchases and, on every iteration, recomputes `sum(earlier.price_cents for earlier in account.purchases[:index + 1])`. That slices and re-sums the whole prefix each time, so it reads n(n+1)/2 prices and makes n slice copies for n purchases. Only the last iteration's value is ever used, and that value is just the sum of all purchases. This is why the account page got slower as histories got longer.
      
      The fix: compute `sum(purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases)` once, which reads each price exactly once, and divide it by `len(account.purchases)` as before. The result is the same as the loop's final value in every case. It is still derived from the purchase list rather than from the carried total_cents, so the existing drifted-total test still holds. An account with no purchases still raises ZeroDivisionError, which render_spend_summary and its test rely on to let the failure reach the request boundary. render_spend_summary and the monthly and typical-spend paths are unchanged.
      
      The test: a new case in tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py passes 200 {F1.1} purchases whose price_cents is a property that counts its reads. It asserts the average is correct and that there are at most 200 {F1.2} reads. Against the old code it would see 20,100 {F1.3} reads.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

      from __future__ import annotations
      
      from io_shop.accounts import Account
      from io_shop.typical_spend import typical_spend_per_item
      
      """What a shopper has spent, and what that averages to.
      
      Three figures about one history. The lifetime average has been on the account
      page for years; the monthly one narrows it to the current month; the typical
      purchase abandons the average altogether for the middle of the history. The
      last two are the ones still behind a rollout, and which of them a request gets
      is decided before it reaches here.
      """
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item across everything this account has ever bought.
      
          Live for years. Its divisor is empty only for an account that has never
          bought anything at all, which no real shopper is.
      
          Derives the total from the purchases rather than reading the one the account
          carries, taking each purchase in and recomputing what has been spent by
          then, so that the figure agrees with the list the shopper is looking at even
          where the totals the query returned have drifted from it.
          """
          spent_by_then = 0 {S1.1}
      
          for index, _ in enumerate(account.purchases):
              spent_by_then = sum(
                  earlier.price_cents for earlier in account.purchases[:index + 1 {S1.2}]
              )
      
          return spent_by_then // len(account.purchases)
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item_this_month(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item this month.
      
          Narrows the lifetime figure to the current month, so the account page can
          show what a shopper is spending now rather than what they averaged over
          three years.
          """
          bought_this_month = [
              purchase for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month
          ]
          return account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)
      
      
      def render_spend_summary(account: Account,
                               use_monthly_summary: bool,
                               use_typical_spend: bool = False) -> int:
          """The figure Io's account page shows, through whichever version the rollout
          selects.
      
          Raises whatever the selected version raises. Catching belongs at the request
          boundary - see `io_shop.account_page` - where there is a response to turn a
          failure into and a log to record it in. A page that swallowed its own errors
          would render a wrong number instead of an error, which is a worse incident
          than the one it hid.
      
          Two rollouts, so two flags to be told about, and the newer one wins where a
          request is inside both. That is the ordinary arrangement: each is a slice of
          traffic, the slices overlap, and the page has to render one figure.
          """
          if use_typical_spend:
              return typical_spend_per_item(account)
      
          if use_monthly_summary:
              return average_spend_per_item_this_month(account)
      
          return average_spend_per_item(account)
      
  - [S2] tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py at 5e07d73
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      import pytest
      from io_shop.accounts import Account, Purchase
      from io_shop.spend_summary import (
          average_spend_per_item,
          average_spend_per_item_this_month,
          render_spend_summary,
      )
      
      """Io's account-page arithmetic - the lifetime figure and the monthly one.
      
      The monthly figure is newer and ships behind a rollout flag, so the cases below
      cover the shape the page has had for years plus the one the flag adds.
      """
      
      
      def an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month(*prices: int) -> Account:
          """The ordinary case: a shopper who has bought before, but not this month."""
          return Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-idle-this-month",
              purchases=tuple(
                  Purchase(price_cents=price, in_current_month=False) for price in prices
              ),
              total_cents=sum(prices),
              total_this_month_cents=0,
          )
      
      
      def test_the_lifetime_average_spreads_the_total_over_every_purchase() -> None:
          account = an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month(1000, 2000 {S2.1}, 3000 {S2.2})
      
          assert average_spend_per_item(account) == 2000 {S2.3}
      
      
      def test_the_lifetime_average_follows_the_purchases_not_the_carried_total() -> None:
          # The figure is derived from the list the shopper is looking at, so a total
          # that has drifted from its own purchases does not reach the page.
          an_account_whose_total_drifted = Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-with-a-stale-total",
              purchases=(
                  Purchase(price_cents=1000, in_current_month=False),
                  Purchase(price_cents=3000, in_current_month=False),
              ),
              total_cents=99_999,
              total_this_month_cents=0,
          )
      
          assert average_spend_per_item(an_account_whose_total_drifted) == 2000 {S2.4}
      
      
      def test_the_monthly_average_is_correct_for_a_shopper_who_did_buy() -> None:
          # The ordinary case for the monthly figure: a shopper who has bought
          # something this month, averaged over what they bought this month.
          an_active_shopper = Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-who-bought-this-month",
              purchases=(
                  Purchase(price_cents=4000, in_current_month=True),
                  Purchase(price_cents=2000, in_current_month=True),
                  Purchase(price_cents=9000, in_current_month=False),
              ),
              total_cents=15000,
              total_this_month_cents=6000,
          )
      
          assert average_spend_per_item_this_month(an_active_shopper) == 3000 {S2.5}
      
      
      def test_the_page_takes_the_stable_summary_when_the_rollout_is_off() -> None:
          account = an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month(1000, 3000 {S2.6})
      
          assert render_spend_summary(account, use_monthly_summary=False) == 2000 {S2.7}
      
      
      def test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller() -> None:
          # Swallowing it here would render a wrong number instead of an error, and
          # there would be no error rate for anyone to alert on.
          a_shopper_who_never_bought_anything = Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-with-no-history", purchases=(), total_cents=0,
              total_this_month_cents=0
          )
      
          with pytest.raises(ZeroDivisionError):
              render_spend_summary(
                  a_shopper_who_never_bought_anything, use_monthly_summary=False
              )

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The rewritten average_spend_per_item, the lifetime-average calculation the account page uses whenever neither rollout flag is set, works out the total from the purchase list instead of reading the total the account already carries. It does this by looping over the purchases and, on every pass, copying and re-summing the whole list up to that point. The work per request therefore grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count, even though only the last pass's sum is used.
cause_in_plain_words: A code change to how the shop works out a shopper's average spend made it add up the shopper's purchases again and again instead of once, so the work grew steeply with the number of things a shopper had bought.
still_at_risk: Account pages could slow down again if revision 5e07d73, or any later revision that still has its spend calculation, is deployed to io-shop.
symptom: Account pages on the shop loaded slowly
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly. The response time of io-shop's slowest requests rose far above its usual level from the onset, while failed requests stayed within their normal variation. (cites AL1; T6, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 2: The slow requests started when io-shop began serving revision 5e07d73. It was deployed during the onset minute, and every replica was running it as of the deployment-status read. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; T11, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 2 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy of revision 70dbcfd. The metrics read back cover the hours from that deploy to the onset and show the service at its normal latency until the onset minute. The service was also measured back to normal once that revision was running again. (cites T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; T6, under "What Argus did, in order"; T22, under "What Argus did, in order"; T23, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: That revision rewrote average_spend_per_item, which render_spend_summary uses for the account page whenever neither rollout flag is set. It now works out the lifetime total from the shopper's purchase list instead of dividing the total the account already carries. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
causal_chain 4: The new loop re-sums the whole purchase list up to each position on every pass, so each account-page request does work that grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count. (cites S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed")
contributing_factors 1: No test was seen that checks how the cost of the account-page spend calculation grows with a long purchase history. The test the change added checks only the result, on an account with a short purchase list.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A test running the calculation on a long purchase history would have shown the quadratic work before the revision was deployed, and the slow pages would never have reached shoppers.
contributing_factors 2: No staged rollout was seen. The revision was running on every io-shop replica as of the deployment-status read, and no step was seen that served it to a slice of traffic and checked latency before the rest.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: A canary with a latency check would have caught the slowdown on a small share of requests and stopped the rollout before every shopper's account page was affected.
action_items 1: Add a CI test that runs the account-page spend calculations (lifetime, monthly and typical) against an account with a long purchase history, and fails when the work grows faster than linearly with the number of purchases. It should run on every change to src/io_shop.
action_items 2: Roll io-shop deployments out to a subset of replicas first, and hold the rest of the rollout until a latency check on that subset passes.
action_items 3: Link the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
went_wrong 1: Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person on call was brought in while the incident ran.
